answer: Yes. The subtext enriches the story naturally rather than feeling forced. Ruth’s “only saying” disguises pressure as casual concern, establishing family expectations within the synagogue community. Leonard’s “You couldn’t have reached him” refers literally to physical distance, while Barbara hears the emotional distance between herself and the troubled boy years earlier. Her promise to her newborn—“I’ll listen to you”—also carries unspoken guilt and uncertainty about whether care can prevent tragedy. These layers deepen the characters and the communal setting without disrupting the story’s action.
